- **Updated**: 2026-10-20T18:38:55Z

## PR Description

## The goal_builder incident (owner-reported)

Reopening the `goal_builder` marathon session (2.7GB JSONL) was slow (30s–3.5min), showed a jumping ctx meter (72% → 21%), and historically dead-ended in an over-window boot loop with endless compaction.

## Root causes found (all reproduced on the real session)

1. **Hidden-checkpoint estimator parity** — when structured compaction hides a `CompactCheckpointRecord` itself, `projection.dart _coverAt` renders its whole span FULL, but both estimators (`estimateProjectedBranchTokens`, `projectedBranchBudgetCut`) still credited its covers: the file priced ~175k while the real request carried ~298k. The resume budget trim never fired → over-window boot → compaction loop. Estimators now mirror the projection exactly (hidden checkpoint covers nothing, renders no marker).
2. **Over-window resume boots instantly** — `_capResumedContext` now applies the `localTrimValve` immediately when the resumed transcript exceeds the window (an LM pass there took minutes on slow summarizers and read as a hung open). Over-trigger-under-window keeps the LM boot cap (gh-1425 contract).
3. **Boot-race wake gate** — `_sessionLoadsInFlight` gates inbox/steering wakes while a marathon load walks: a wake run against the half-loaded agent died on the over-window guard before the boot cap could run.
4. **2.7GB primary scan on the boot path** — the windowed storage never rotates, so the orphan-report seed (`lastSegmentOnly`) and the steering/obligations/registry scans read the whole giant from offset 0 (~12–30s of every open). `readCustomRecordsOfType` now tail-caps each file at `kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes` (all consumers are tail consumers); deep-history callers pass `tailCapBytes: null`.

## Measured on the real 2.7GB session (headless probe)

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| open → first turn start | ~31–32s | **3.7s** |
| full probe run (boot + 174k prefill + answer) | 1m51s | ~7s (prefill rides the provider cache afterwards) |
| bogus compaction at open | yes (meter jumps, boot cap churn) | none (174k < 183k trigger — correctly skipped) |

## Tests

- `test/compaction/token_estimation_test.dart` — hidden-checkpoint parity group
- `test/cli/agent_cli_resume_boot_cap_test.dart` — instant-trim boot (0 LM calls), degraded summarizer, crashed-report backstop, stale-abort
- `test/cli/agent_cli_inbox_wake_test.dart` — wake defers while a session load is in flight
- `test/session/custom_record_tail_cap_test.dart` — tail-capped raw scans

Plus a drive-by: macOS FSEvents flake fix in `config_section_preservation_reg_test.dart` (late replay of save #1's tmp-file events blamed save #2; CI/Linux never saw it).

# pr-1726: fix: goal_builder resume — hidden-checkpoint estimator parity, instant over-window boot cap, wake gate, tail-capped boot scans

## Description

## The goal_builder incident (owner-reported)

Reopening the `goal_builder` marathon session (2.7GB JSONL) was slow (30s–3.5min), showed a jumping ctx meter (72% → 21%), and historically dead-ended in an over-window boot loop with endless compaction.

## Root causes found (all reproduced on the real session)

1. **Hidden-checkpoint estimator parity** — when structured compaction hides a `CompactCheckpointRecord` itself, `projection.dart _coverAt` renders its whole span FULL, but both estimators (`estimateProjectedBranchTokens`, `projectedBranchBudgetCut`) still credited its covers: the file priced ~175k while the real request carried ~298k. The resume budget trim never fired → over-window boot → compaction loop. Estimators now mirror the projection exactly (hidden checkpoint covers nothing, renders no marker).
2. **Over-window resume boots instantly** — `_capResumedContext` now applies the `localTrimValve` immediately when the resumed transcript exceeds the window (an LM pass there took minutes on slow summarizers and read as a hung open). Over-trigger-under-window keeps the LM boot cap (gh-1425 contract).
3. **Boot-race wake gate** — `_sessionLoadsInFlight` gates inbox/steering wakes while a marathon load walks: a wake run against the half-loaded agent died on the over-window guard before the boot cap could run.
4. **2.7GB primary scan on the boot path** — the windowed storage never rotates, so the orphan-report seed (`lastSegmentOnly`) and the steering/obligations/registry scans read the whole giant from offset 0 (~12–30s of every open). `readCustomRecordsOfType` now tail-caps each file at `kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes` (all consumers are tail consumers); deep-history callers pass `tailCapBytes: null`.

## Measured on the real 2.7GB session (headless probe)

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| open → first turn start | ~31–32s | **3.7s** |
| full probe run (boot + 174k prefill + answer) | 1m51s | ~7s (prefill rides the provider cache afterwards) |
| bogus compaction at open | yes (meter jumps, boot cap churn) | none (174k < 183k trigger — correctly skipped) |

## Tests

- `test/compaction/token_estimation_test.dart` — hidden-checkpoint parity group
- `test/cli/agent_cli_resume_boot_cap_test.dart` — instant-trim boot (0 LM calls), degraded summarizer, crashed-report backstop, stale-abort
- `test/cli/agent_cli_inbox_wake_test.dart` — wake defers while a session load is in flight
- `test/session/custom_record_tail_cap_test.dart` — tail-capped raw scans

Plus a drive-by: macOS FSEvents flake fix in `config_section_preservation_reg_test.dart` (late replay of save #1's tmp-file events blamed save #2; CI/Linux never saw it).

# pr-1726: fix: goal_builder resume — hidden-checkpoint estimator parity, instant over-window boot cap, wake gate, tail-capped boot scans

## Description

## The goal_builder incident (owner-reported)

Reopening the `goal_builder` marathon session (2.7GB JSONL) was slow (30s–3.5min), showed a jumping ctx meter (72% → 21%), and historically dead-ended in an over-window boot loop with endless compaction.

## Root causes found (all reproduced on the real session)

1. **Hidden-checkpoint estimator parity** — when structured compaction hides a `CompactCheckpointRecord` itself, `projection.dart _coverAt` renders its whole span FULL, but both estimators (`estimateProjectedBranchTokens`, `projectedBranchBudgetCut`) still credited its covers: the file priced ~175k while the real request carried ~298k. The resume budget trim never fired → over-window boot → compaction loop. Estimators now mirror the projection exactly (hidden checkpoint covers nothing, renders no marker).
2. **Over-window resume boots instantly** — `_capResumedContext` now applies the `localTrimValve` immediately when the resumed transcript exceeds the window (an LM pass there took minutes on slow summarizers and read as a hung open). Over-trigger-under-window keeps the LM boot cap (gh-1425 contract).
3. **Boot-race wake gate** — `_sessionLoadsInFlight` gates inbox/steering wakes while a marathon load walks: a wake run against the half-loaded agent died on the over-window guard before the boot cap could run.
4. **2.7GB primary scan on the boot path** — the windowed storage never rotates, so the orphan-report seed (`lastSegmentOnly`) and the steering/obligations/registry scans read the whole giant from offset 0 (~12–30s of every open). `readCustomRecordsOfType` now tail-caps each file at `kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes` (all consumers are tail consumers); deep-history callers pass `tailCapBytes: null`.

## Measured on the real 2.7GB session (headless probe)

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| open → first turn start | ~31–32s | **3.7s** |
| full probe run (boot + 174k prefill + answer) | 1m51s | ~7s (prefill rides the provider cache afterwards) |
| bogus compaction at open | yes (meter jumps, boot cap churn) | none (174k < 183k trigger — correctly skipped) |

## Tests

- `test/compaction/token_estimation_test.dart` — hidden-checkpoint parity group
- `test/cli/agent_cli_resume_boot_cap_test.dart` — instant-trim boot (0 LM calls), degraded summarizer, crashed-report backstop, stale-abort
- `test/cli/agent_cli_inbox_wake_test.dart` — wake defers while a session load is in flight
- `test/session/custom_record_tail_cap_test.dart` — tail-capped raw scans

Plus a drive-by: macOS FSEvents flake fix in `config_section_preservation_reg_test.dart` (late replay of save #1's tmp-file events blamed save #2; CI/Linux never saw it).

No: you can't hide a record that doesn't exist yet. So the checkpoint is always OLDER than the hide record → in the backward walk, the hide record is encountered FIRST. ✓. Window 32768 (the small `_model`). `tokens > 32768`? ~4k? After trim: budget = min(keepRecentTokens, max(0, 32768 - reserve - overhead - 64)) — lands under trigger 26214ish. The turn request ≤ _threshold ✓.

5. One more thing to check — `_capResumedContext` runs where relative to `_sessionLoadsInFlight` decrement: inside `_loadSessionInner` (called at line 738 `await _capResumedContext(session)`) — within the try block → the counter stays > 0 while the boot cap runs, including the LM path. ✓ Gate covers the whole cap.

6. What about a wake that fires between `_session = await _loadSession(...)` completing and... fine.

7. Steering recovery scan (`agent_cli_stering.dart:459`) runs at boot inside `_loadSessionInner`? It's the boot steering recovery — gated anyway.

8. `child_session_io.dart` subagentRegistryRows — called when? task listing — post-boot. Tail-capped now — records.last — registry snapshots: latest wins. Fine.

9. One potential correctness issue with the tail cap: **stering consumed-before-pending across the cap boundary**. Actually wait, I need to double-check one scenario: pending steering record OLDER than the cap boundary (dropped), consumed record NEWER (kept) → fine (consumed seen, pending absent → nothing recovered — correct, it was consumed). Pending INSIDE, consumed OUTSIDE (older)? Impossible: consumed is written after pending. OK.

But what about the obligations ledger? `records.last` — ledger snapshots are full-replacement payloads (fromPayload of the LAST). Older snapshots dropped — fine (latest wins).

Orphan-report seed: `lastSegmentOnly: true` — last segment's tail. reportedOrphanKeys — keys seen; dropping older keys = a re-report possibility — pre-accepted trade (comment says so).

10. `readCustomRecordsOfType` on a file SMALLER than the cap: offset = max(0, size - 95MB) = 0 — full scan, unchanged behavior ✓.

11. `kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes` = 95MB default cap vs design "80MB rotate / 95MB hard-cap" — rotated .part files ≤ 80MB < 95MB → scanned in full ✓ (comment says so).

12. Edge: what if a single custom record is LARGER than the tail cap (e.g., a giant obligations snapshot > 95MB)? Its line spans the boundary; the scan starts mid-line → decode fails → skipped → the LATEST snapshot silently missing → records.last = an OLDER snapshot → stale obligations resurrect? For the obligations ledger, an older snapshot could miss pending-wait records → obligations lost. Realistic? A 95MB single JSON line — unlikely (obligations snapshots are small). The 2.7GB session's records are per-turn messages, not custom records. Marginal; not worth flaging beyond a note in the tail-cap comment (maybe SUGESTION).

Not in the diff (23 files, no crap4dart.yaml). The `--only-down` guard compares thresholds, not per-function scores. The `localTrimValve` extraction might change complexity metrics but the gate is about config thresholds. OK.

- The PR description states: "readCustomRecordsOfType now tail-caps each file at kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes (all consumers are tail consumers); deep-history callers pass tailCapBytes: null."
- Implementation: `final cap = tailCapBytes ?? kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes;` — `null` → 95MB cap. The described opt-out does NOT exist. The dead `tailCapBytes == null ? 0` branch in `_readCustomRecordsStreamed` is unreachable from the public API.
- The new test comment asserts "Explicit unbounded: the whole file is scanned (deep-history callers opt out of the cap)" — misleading test (passes vacuously since the fixture is 70KB ≪ 95MB).

Is this BLOCKING (correctness/bug — "broken behavior") or IMPORTANT? The contract is broken but no current caller passes null; today's behavior is exactly "everything capped at 95MB" which the PR intends for all existing consumers. The broken piece is only the ADVERTISED escape hatch. Since the machine protocol says BLOCKING = "merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break" — no bug fires today. → ⚠️ IMPORTANT, sharply worded: "the documented null opt-out is a silent no-op; either implement the sentinel or fix the docs/test comment."

Hmm, wait. Let me think about whether the author INTENDED null = default and the description is just wrong. The dead branch `tailCapBytes == null ? 0` proves the streamed reader was written to support null = unbounded. The wrapper defeats it. So it IS an implementation bug (dead code + broken contract), just one without a current victim. IMPORTANT with a strong recommendation. Actually — hold on. Could `readCustomRecordsOfType` itself be called with `tailCapBytes: null` by EXTERNAL consumers (it's a public method on the public JsonlSessionRepo)? Yes — flutter_agent_harness is a published package; external hosts calling with null expecting unbounded get 95MB silently. Still no in-repo victim. IMPORTANT.

Scope creep StreamTrace: the commit "feat(providers): StreamTrace diagnostic" is unrelated to goal_builder resume and absent from the PR description (which even lists its test files' peers but not stream_trace tests). Per review guidelines: flag deviations unless justified → ⚠️ IMPORTANT.

Hmm — actually wait. Let me re-read the PR description "Tests" list: token_estimation, resume_boot_cap, inbox_wake, custom_record_tail_cap + FSEvents drive-by. No mention of StreamTrace AT ALL (neither feature nor its 2 test files). And "Files Changed: 23" — the description doesn't enumerate. So yes: undocumented feature riding a fix PR = scope creep → IMPORTANT (it does not break anything; it's off by default and tested).

Now the FSEvents test change: 100ms→150ms delay adds 1.4s to that test on ALL platforms (CI time). Fine, minor. It's declared in the description. OK.

Now let me also double-check the AC3 rewrite didn't weaken the gh-1425 contract: "Over-trigger-under-window keeps the LM boot cap" — the code: `if (tokens > _effectiveContextWindow)` → instant trim; else (trigger < tokens ≤ window) → LM pass. ✓ matches.

One more check on `localTrimValve`: the reason string interpolation: `'$localTrimMarkerPrefix $reason, $cut older message(s)...'` → for the compactor path: "…[context trimmed] the summarizer endpoint was unavailable, 5 older message(s) were dropped…" — identical to old text ✓ (old: `'$localTrimMarkerPrefix the summarizer endpoint was unavailable, '$cut older...`). Byte-identical for the old call path ✓.

Check `localTrimMarkerPrefix` still referenced in auto_compactor.dart (it's a const somewhere) ✓ compiles.

Also: `estimateTokens(messages.last)` inside localTrimValve — same as before ✓.

Anything about `localTrimValve` being called in `_capResumedContext` with `_effectiveCompactionSettings` — the same settings the boot cap uses ✓.

Wake gate placement in `_wakeOnInboxMail`: BEFORE the gh-1180 lane decision. Mail stays pending — but does the streak/chatter logic misbehave when deferred? No — it just returns; next tick re-evaluates. ✓

One more: `_sessionLoadsInFlight` is not reset on `/exit` or session switch failure — `finally` handles exceptions. If `_loadSession` is cancelled (zone?), finally still runs. ✓

Potential deadlock: inbox wake deferred while load in flight; the load itself waits on nothing from the inbox. No cycle. ✓

Let me now check job 2 (CLI tests). And also double check `provider_common.dart` `data.length` context (what type `data` is).

Key observations so far:

**Scope creep**: The PR title/description does NOT mention StreamTrace (commit 6a55bbc57b "feat(providers): StreamTrace diagnostic"). That's an unrelated diagnostic feature bundled in a fix PR. Now, deep-dive areas to verify:

### 1. `localTrimValve` extraction
The refactoring moved `_localTrimFallback` logic to a top-level function `localTrimValve`. Behavior parity check:
- Old: marker text `'the summarizer endpoint was unavailable, $cut older message(s)...'`
- New: parameterized `reason` — `'the summarizer endpoint was unavailable'` for the compactor path; `'the resumed transcript exceeded the context window'` for boot cap. Text identical modulo reason. Good.
- `final overhead = overheadTokens;` — redundant local variable. Minor style nit (SUGESTION). Actually it keeps the comment context. It's fine but slightly awkward.
- One subtle difference: in old code, `overhead` was computed inside the function from `state.systemPrompt`/`state.tools`. Now passed in. Same for boot-cap call site. OK.

Interesting: in `auto_compactor.dart`, there's an accidental blank-line change at line ~810: the doc comment for `AutoCompactorSources` — "skips the smol→main fallback (one attempt only —\n+\n retrying the same call wouldn't help)." ``
 /// summarizers and skips the smol→main fallback (one attempt only —
+
 /// retrying the same call wouldn't help).
``

That inserts a blank line between two lines of a `///` doc comment. This splits the doc comment into two docs — the second line "/// retrying the same call wouldn't help)." becomes a separate dangling doc comment attached to... hmm. Actually in Dart, `///` lines form one doc comment contiguous block; a blank non-`///` line breaks the block. So the doc comment now ends at "(one attempt only —" and the `/// retrying the same call wouldn't help).` line starts a NEW dangling doc comment which is attached to... the next declaration? The next declaration would be `class AutoCompactorSources {`? Wait no, the blank `+` line is between. Let me check the actual file.

Actually a dangling `///` comment before a blank line and then a class... Let me read the real file to see. Actually `/// retrying the same call wouldn't help).` is followed by `class AutoCompactorSources {`. Hmm, no — need to check ordering. The diff hunk:

``

So yes — a blank line was inserted in the middle of the `///` doc comment for `AutoCompactorSources`. This produces a dangling library-style doc comment warning? In Dart, `///` comments must be attached to a declaration. The first block `/// The smol/main summarizer sources...` is attached to the class (still, because blank line inside doesn't break attachment? Actually it DOES split into two comment blocks. The first block attaches to... the blank line then `/// retrying...` then `class`. The second block `/// retrying the same call wouldn't help).` attaches to `class AutoCompactorSources`. The FIRST block becomes dangling (not attached to any declaration) → analyzer warning `dangling_library_doc_comments`. This looks like an accidental keystroke from the edit. Let me verify in the file and run the analyzer.

This is a real finding — likely an unintentional edit (accidental). Severity: SUGESTION/IMPORTANT. If analyzer flags it and CI runs `dart analyze` as a gate, it could be BLOCKING via red CI. ### 2. Boot cap instant trim (`agent_cli_compaction.dart`)
```dart
if (tokens > _effectiveContextWindow) {
 final trimmed = localTrimValve(...);
 if (trimmed != null) {

This PR is titled and described as the `goal_builder` resume fix (estimator parity, instant boot cap, wake gate, tail-capped scans). It also ships an **entirely unrelated new diagnostic feature — StreamTrace (~400 lines)** — that is absent from the title, the PR description, the root-cause list, and the test list:

- new `lib/src/providers/stream_trace.dart` (+87) and `stream_trace_io.dart` (+54)
- new public API exported from **two barrels**: `flutter_agent_harness.dart:200` and `io.dart`

The code itself looks fine (off by default, analyzer-clean, well tested — I ran the new tests, all green). The problem is process and reviewability: a reviewer cannot approve what the author never declared, and this public-API surface lands in a published package with no changelog entry and no motivation anywhere in the PR.

**Fix (either is acceptable):**
1. Split the StreamTrace work into its own PR (`feat(providers): StreamTrace diagnostic`) with its own description/tests/changelog entry, keeping this PR the targeted incident fix; **or**
2. Keep it here but document it: add StreamTrace to the PR title/description (root causes/tests), and add a `## Unreleased` CHANGELOG line for the new public API and the `FA_STREAM_TRACE` knob.

arguments.content:
⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the `tailCapBytes: null` opt-out is a silent no-op — the documented unbounded scan does not exist**

`readCustomRecordsOfType` documents (and the PR description repeats) that deep-history callers pass `tailCapBytes: null` to escape the cap:

```dart
// session_repo.dart:841-842
// smaller than that and scan in full. Deep-history callers pass
// `tailCapBytes: null`.
final cap = tailCapBytes ?? kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes;
```

`?? kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes` makes `null` **identical to omitting the parameter** — both cap at 95 MB. There is no way to request an unbounded scan through this API anymore, and the unbounded branch in the streamed reader is dead code, unreachable from the public API:

```dart
// session_repo.dart:921-922
var offset = tailCapBytes == null   // never null: `cap` above is never null
    ? 0
    : math.max(0, size - tailCapBytes);
```

The new test even asserts the broken contract — `test/session/custom_record_tail_cap_test.dart:59-66` comments "Explicit unbounded: the whole file is scanned (deep-history callers opt out of the cap)" and expects both records with `tailCapBytes: null` — but it passes **vacuously**: the ~70 KB fixture is far below the 95 MB default, so `offset` clamps to 0 either way. The test cannot distinguish "null = unbounded" from "null = default cap".

No in-repo caller passes `tailCapBytes` today (I checked all five: obligations latest, orphan-report seed, steering recovery, subagent registry, the `customRecordScan` fallback — all tail consumers), so no behavior regresses **today**. But the first deep-history caller to follow the documented contract will silently scan only the last 95 MB of a giant primary and miss everything older — exactly the silent-truncation class this parameter exists to opt out of.

**Suggested fix** — make the sentinel real (distinguish "not passed" from "explicitly unbounded"):

```dart
Future<List<CustomRecord>> readCustomRecordsOfType(
  SessionMetadata metadata,
  Set<String> types, {
  bool lastSegmentOnly = false,
  int? tailCapBytes = kSessionSegmentHardCapBytes, // null = unbounded
})
```

and drop the `??` coalescing. Then add a fixture that actually crosses the cap (e.g. `debugCustomRecordScanBlockBytes` shrink + a >cap file) so the unbounded path is exercised, not vacuous. Alternatively, if `null` was never meant to be the opt-out, fix the doc comment at line 841, the PR description, and the test comment — but then the dead `tailCapBytes == null` branch at line 921 should go too.

No: you can't hide a record that doesn't exist yet. So the checkpoint is always OLDER than the hide record → in the backward walk, the hide record is encountered FIRST. ✓. 💡 **SUGGESTION: StreamTrace install — `HOME` gate never arms on Windows; doc cites a non-existent `Platform.environment.lookup`**

Two nits on the wiring at this hunk:

Update the doc to match reality.

Also worth a line in the doc: the sink **truncates** `~/.fah/logs/stream-trace.log` on every armed start (`FileStreamTraceSink` ctor) — one `fa` run destroys the previous run's trace, which surprises anyone collecting traces across runs.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: StreamTrace install — `HOME` gate never arms on Windows; doc cites a non-existent `Platform.environment.lookup`**

arguments.content:
💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: StreamTrace install — `HOME` gate never arms on Windows; doc cites a non-existent `Platform.environment.lookup`**

Two nits on the wiring at this hunk:

Also worth a line in the doc: the sink **truncates** `~/.fah/logs/stream-trace.log` on every armed start (`FileStreamTraceSink` ctor) — one `fa` run destroys the previous run's trace, which surprises anyone collecting traces across runs.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.

2. **Doc references a non-existent member.** `stream_trace_io.dart:46-47` says "real hosts pass `Platform.environment.lookup`" — `Platform.environment` is a plain `Map<String, String>` with no `lookup` member; the actual wiring here passes a `(key) => Platform.environment[key]` closure. Update the doc to match reality.

Also worth a line in the doc: the sink **truncates** `~/.fah/logs/stream-trace.log` on every armed start (`FileStreamTraceSink` ctor) — one `fa` run destroys the previous run's trace, which surprises anyone collecting traces across runs.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: StreamTrace install — `HOME` gate never arms on Windows; doc cites a non-existent `Platform.environment.lookup`**

Two nits on the wiring at this hunk:

1. **Windows never traces.** `Platform.environment['HOME']` is unset on Windows (it is `USERPROFILE` / `LOCALAPPDATA` there), so `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1` silently arms nothing on that platform — the knob is a no-op for Windows hosts and, worse, silently so. Consider `Platform.environment['HOME'] ?? Platform.environment['USERPROFILE']`, or let `maybeStartStreamTrace` take an already-resolved directory.

2. **Doc references a non-existent member.** `stream_trace_io.dart:46-47` says "real hosts pass `Platform.environment.lookup`" — `Platform.environment` is a plain `Map<String, String>` with no `lookup` member; the actual wiring here passes a `(key) => Platform.environment[key]` closure. Update the doc to match reality.

Also worth a line in the doc: the sink **truncates** `~/.fah/logs/stream-trace.log` on every armed start (`FileStreamTraceSink` ctor) — one `fa` run destroys the previous run's trace, which surprises anyone collecting traces across runs.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: StreamTrace install — `HOME` gate never arms on Windows; doc cites a non-existent `Platform.environment.lookup`**

Two nits on the wiring at this hunk:

1. **Windows never traces.** `Platform.environment['HOME']` is unset on Windows (it is `USERPROFILE` / `LOCALAPPDATA` there), so `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1` silently arms nothing on that platform — the knob is a no-op for Windows hosts and, worse, silently so. Consider `Platform.environment['HOME'] ?? Platform.environment['USERPROFILE']`, or let `maybeStartStreamTrace` take an already-resolved directory.

2. **Doc references a non-existent member.** `stream_trace_io.dart:46-47` says "real hosts pass `Platform.environment.lookup`" — `Platform.environment` is a plain `Map<String, String>` with no `lookup` member; the actual wiring here passes a `(key) => Platform.environment[key]` closure. Update the doc to match reality.

Also worth a line in the doc: the sink **truncates** `~/.fah/logs/stream-trace.log` on every armed start (`FileStreamTraceSink` ctor) — one `fa` run destroys the previous run's trace, which surprises anyone collecting traces across runs.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: per-chunk synchronous `flush: true` writes on the hot stream path**

`FileStreamTraceSink.writeLine` performs a synchronous open-append-**flush** per mark, and the marks sit on the hottest path in the provider pipeline (`net` per SSE byte-chunk in `createSseIterator`, `emit` per delta in `AssistantMessageEventStream.push`, `render` per TUI write) — i.e. up to **three sync fsync-class writes per streamed delta** while `FA_STREAM_TRACE=1`.

For an opt-in diagnostic this is acceptable, and the silent-on-failure contract is right. But on a bursty endpoint the trace itself perturbs the very latency it measures (each flush can cost milliseconds and stalls the event loop between chunks). If the trace is meant for cadence post-mortems, consider buffering lines and flushing on a short timer (e.g. every 250 ms) or on `stop()` — the "no pending async writes a crash can lose" guarantee matters less for a timing trail than for the fa.log telemetry sink it cites.
